To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sidebranching amplitude in a phase field model of crystal growth is amplified by the same mechanism as predicted by the linear WKB theory, and that this mechanism is consistent with the fluctuation spectrum of the interface in thermal equilibrium.

(1) the phase field model of dendrite growth with thermal noise predicts a fluctuation spectrum in thermal equilibrium which is in quantitative agreement with the exact sharp interfacial spectrum up to the interface width, and (2) the model of dendritic growth with thermal noise reproduces the linear theory of sidebranching in quantitative detail, and thus is a viable candidate for explaining the observed large amplitude sidebranching in the experiments of Trivedi et al.

the sidebranching amplitude increases with distance behind the tip as a power law with an exponent of 0.5 in two dimensions, and that the sidebranch spacing decreases with distance behind the tips as a power law of 1/3 in three dimensions.

the phase field approach is a powerful tool to investigate the role of thermal noise on dendritic growth, which is important for understanding of dendritic sidebranches and dendritic growth in general.
the noise in the phase field model is a reasonable approximation of thermal noise, and that the noise is amplified by the same mechanism as in the sharp interface model.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the linear theory of noise amplficiation is quantitatively correct, and that this theory can be used to predict the noise level in dendritic growth.

the linear WKB theory is a good quantitative approximation of the noise spectrum in the phase field model, and that the phase field model is a promising tool for studying the effects of microscopic noise on dendritic sidebranch formation.
the WKB theory of dendritic growth in the presence of thermal noise is quantitatively correct, at least for the case where noise is the dominant source of fluctuations.
